title: Bad Estimates from a Local Variable: OPTION (RECOMPILE)
description: A local-variable 'unknown' estimate picks a scan a real value wouldn't; OPTION(RECOMPILE) lets the optimizer see the value and seek.
narrative:
## Scenario
`DECLARE @s VARCHAR(12) = 'Open'; SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, Total FROM Orders WHERE Status = @s;` returns only ~200 rows (the `Status` values are heavily skewed), yet the plan is a full **Clustered Index Scan** of all 300,000 rows.

## Why it's slow
The value lives in a **local variable**. At compile time SQL Server cannot see what `@s` holds, so instead of using the histogram it falls back to the **density vector** — the *average* rows-per-value across all statuses (~100,000). Believing 100,000 rows will match, it decides the non-covering `IX_Orders_Status` seek would trigger 100,000 key lookups and rejects it, scanning the whole table instead. This is the same estimation trap as classic **parameter sniffing**: the plan is built for a guessed cardinality, not the real one.

## What to look for
- A **Clustered Index Scan** even though the predicate is highly selective.
- Reads far larger than the handful of rows returned — the estimate, not reality, drove the plan.

## The concept
Add `OPTION (RECOMPILE)`. It recompiles at execution time and **embeds the literal value** of `@s`, so the optimizer probes the histogram for `'Open'` specifically, estimates ~200 rows, and switches to an **Index Seek** with a key lookup. `RECOMPILE` trades a little extra CPU per run for an accurate, value-specific plan — ideal for queries over skewed data.
startingQuery: DECLARE @s VARCHAR(12) = 'Open'; SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, Total FROM Orders WHERE Status = @s;
hints: The value is in a local variable, so the optimizer can't sniff it and uses the average (density) estimate instead of the histogram.
That average estimate (~100k rows) is wildly wrong for the rare 'Open' status, so it scans instead of seeking.
Add OPTION (RECOMPILE) so SQL Server recompiles with the actual value embedded and re-estimates from the histogram.
